items.canonical_answer: A measure of changes in the cost of a representative consumer basket relative to a base period.
marking_guidance: Definition/key term (1): representative basket price change against a base.

items.prompt: Calculate the Year 1 price index with base 100 from an invented identical basket costing N$500 in the base year and N$550 in Year 1.
items.canonical_answer: Index = current basket cost / base cost × 100 = 550 / 500 × 100 = 110.
marking_guidance: Formula/substitution (1): 550/500×100. Result/units interpretation (1): index 110, not N$110.

items.prompt: Analyse the annual price change where an invented index rises from 110 to 115.5, base 100 unchanged.
items.canonical_answer: It rises 5.5 index points. The proportionate increase is 5.5/110 = 0.05, equivalent to 5%, rather than 5.5% or 15.5% over this year.
marking_guidance: Pattern (1): index increases. Evidence (1): 5.5 points. Explanation (2): use earlier 110 denominator (1), gives 5% annual rise (1).

items.canonical_answer: A sustained rise in the general price level.
marking_guidance: Definition/key term (1): sustained general price rise.

items.prompt: Explain the distinction between demand-pull and cost-push inflation by their initiating causes.
items.canonical_answer: Demand-pull begins with spending pressure beyond responsive capacity; cost-push begins with higher production costs passed into general prices.
marking_guidance: Difference (1): demand relative to capacity. Contrast/test (1): production-cost pressure.

items.prompt: Explain the supported inflation cause where imported input costs rise broadly and firms raise selling prices despite unchanged customer demand.
items.canonical_answer: This is cost-push pressure: higher production costs initiate the general-price increase, rather than stronger demand.
marking_guidance: Context (1): broad input cost increase. Reason/conclusion (1): costs rather than demand initiate price pressure.

items.prompt: Explain the effect of 10% relevant price inflation on an invented fixed N$3,000 monthly pension, with no other income adjustment.
items.canonical_answer: The previous bundle would cost N$3,300. The pension remains N$3,000, so purchasing power falls and the recipient must reduce quantities or other spending to accommodate higher prices.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): relevant prices rise. Because/mechanism (2): old bundle now N$3,300 (1), money income fixed (1). Consequence (1): less purchasing power.

items.prompt: Explain why unexpected inflation does not automatically improve loan affordability for a debtor whose money income and fixed nominal repayment stay unchanged while essentials become dearer.
items.canonical_answer: The debt’s real value may fall, but its cash repayment does not. Higher essential costs leave less income for repayment, so practical affordability can worsen.
marking_guidance: Context (1): fixed income/repayment and dearer essentials. Reason/conclusion (1): real debt reduction differs from budget affordability.

items.prompt: Define retail price index (2). Identify the causes in these invented cases: spending rises beyond available output; broad input costs rise and are passed on (2). Explain an effect of 10% basket inflation on a fixed money pension (2). Identify the base and current basket costs from this invented comparison: base N$500, current N$550 (2).
items.canonical_answer: The index compares a representative basket’s cost with a base. The cases show demand-pull and cost-push inflation. A fixed pension buys less after prices rise, requiring an adjustment in consumption. The basket costs are N$500 base and N$550 current.
marking_guidance: Meaning (2): representative basket price measure (1), base comparison (1). Separate points for causes (2): demand-pull (1), cost-push (1). Explanation (2): fixed money income (1), lower purchasing power (1). Identification (2): base N$500 (1), current N$550 (1). Marks allocation 8.

items.prompt: Invented identical basket costs: base year N$500, Year 1 N$550, Year 2 N$577.50. A general rise in imported input costs occurs with customer demand unchanged. Household A receives a fixed N$3,000 monthly pension. Household B has fixed nominal debt and repayment; its money income rises 10% while its relevant prices rise 5%. No contract repricing or other changes are assumed. Describe three features: base index, Year 2 index and the initiating inflation cause (6). Explain the annual inflation calculation and the cost-push mechanism (7). Discuss whether the two households are affected equally (7).
items.canonical_answer: Base index is 100, Year 2 index 115.5 and cost-push begins with broad imported input costs. Annual inflation in Year 2 is 5.5/110, equivalent to 5%; price levels still rise. Input costs passed into prices explain cost-push with unchanged demand. A loses purchasing power; B’s fixed repayment takes a smaller income share while income outpaces prices. Effects differ, conditional on the stated fixed contract and relevant baskets.
marking_guidance: Data description (6): base reference (1), 100 detail (1); Year 2 index (1), 115.5 detail (1); cost-push (1), input-cost detail (1). Mechanism/explanation (7): Year 1 index 110 (1), change 5.5 points (1), earlier 110 denominator (1), 5% annual rate (1); input cost rises (1), firms pass through (1), general prices rise without demand growth (1). Both sides/judgement (7): A fixed income (1), purchasing power falls (1); B income rises faster than prices (1), fixed repayment smaller income share (1); condition contract unchanged/personal baskets (1); judgement unequal effects (1), tied to income adjustment and debt terms (1). Marks allocation 6+7+7=20.

facts: Invented identical basket costs: base year N$500, Year 1 N$550, Year 2 N$577.50. A general rise in imported input costs occurs with customer demand unchanged. Household A receives a fixed N$3,000 monthly pension. Household B has fixed nominal debt and repayment; its money income rises 10% while its relevant prices rise 5%. No contract repricing or other changes are assumed.

items.prompt: Invented 10% relevant price inflation. Case 1: pension income stays N$3,000 monthly, no other resources change. Case 2: a debtor’s fixed nominal balance and fixed cash repayment do not change; money income rises 10% and no interest repricing or other costs occur. Both have the same relevant price rise. Evaluate the inflation effect on the pensioner (7). Evaluate the claim that the debtor benefits (7), distinguishing nominal debt, real debt and affordability.
items.canonical_answer: Case 1: pension money is unchanged but the old bundle costs N$3,300, so real consumption capacity falls. The impact could be smaller with a different basket or compensating resources, but neither is supplied. Case 2: nominal debt is unchanged, its real purchasing-power value falls, and repayment takes a smaller share of rising income. A benefit is supported under these fixed-contract conditions, although other debtors with fixed incomes or repriced rates might not gain.
marking_guidance: Case 1 marks (7): argument for adverse effect fixed income (1), old bundle N$3,300 (1); limiting argument personal basket may differ (1), compensation could change outcome (1); condition none supplied (1); judgement purchasing-power loss (1), tied to fixed income (1). Case 2 allocation (7): argument for lower real debt (1), lower repayment/income share (1); argument against nominal sum still due (1), other contract/income cases differ (1); condition income rise and fixed contract (1); judgement benefit supported here (1), separate real value from nominal and affordability (1). Total 14.
